{"title":"One-to-Many Relationships (Django)","body":"Start by recalling that you have already defined models and fields, and you have seen how Django creates a table for each model. What you have not yet formalised is how rows in one table can be associated with many rows in another.

In the shop example on page 547, the shop_product table contains a category_id column that stores the primary key of a Category row. Each product points to exactly one category, but a single category row can appear in the category_id column of many product rows – that is the essence of a one‑to‑many relationship.

You will need this idea when you later filter products by category or display all products belonging to a category, because Django’s ORM uses the foreign key to follow the relationship in both directions.

To check that the class has grasped it, ask: “If I give you one Category, can it be linked to more than one Product?” A correct “yes” indicates they understand the one‑to‑many pattern."}
